title: Time, Speed & Distance
relevance: Core aptitude topic in campus OAs and assessment centers; relative-speed reasoning is often disguised as trains, boats, races, patrols, or shuttling drones.
company_notes: Assessment centers such as Cisco, Microsoft, or Optiver often hide standard relative-speed formulas behind patrol agents, clock hands, or data packets.

phases.goal: Establish the core speed–distance–time relations, unit conversion, average speed, and relative speed.

must_hit.point: Speed equals distance divided by time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States Speed = Distance / Time as the defining relation.

must_hit.point: 1 km/h equals 5/18 m/s; convert m/s to km/h by multiplying by 18/5.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives both conversion directions with the 5/18 and 18/5 factors.

must_hit.point: Average speed is total distance over total time; for two equal distances at speeds a and b it is 2ab/(a+b).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects arithmetic averaging of speeds and cites the equal-distance formula 2ab/(a+b).

must_hit.point: Relative speed is S1+S2 in opposite directions and |S1−S2| in the same direction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both opposite-direction sum and same-direction absolute difference.

must_hit.point: If new speed is a/b of usual speed, new time is b/a of usual time; delay is (b/a − 1)T.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses inverse proportion of speed and time and the delay formula (b/a − 1)T.

probes: What is average speed when you cover equal distances at two different speeds?
How do you convert between km/h and m/s, and when do you add versus subtract speeds?

hints.1: Start from Speed = Distance / Time and say what average speed actually means.
hints.2: Separate unit conversion, equal-distance average speed, and relative speed by direction.
hints.3: State 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s, average = 2ab/(a+b) for equal distances, and opposite/same relative speeds S1+S2 and |S1−S2|.

phases.goal: Apply relative speed and length rules to trains, boats/streams, races, and circular tracks.

must_hit.point: A train passing a man or pole covers its own length; passing a platform covers train length plus platform length.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses train length alone for a pole/man and train+platform for a platform, with relative speed if the man moves.

must_hit.point: Two equal-length trains passing in the same direction cover 2L at relative speed |S1−S2|.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says distance to pass is sum of lengths (2L when equal) at same-direction relative speed.

must_hit.point: Downstream speed is u+v and upstream is u−v; still-water and stream speeds are (D+U)/2 and (D−U)/2.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes D=u+v, U=u−v and recovers u and v from the averages of D and U.

must_hit.point: In a race, when A finishes, B's distance at that time gives how far A beats B; 'beats by metres or seconds' links the loser's leftover distance to that time gap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Computes B's position when A finishes, or converts 'beats by m or s' into B's speed and A's time.

must_hit.point: On a circular track, the k-th meeting occurs when relative distance covered is k times track length; same-direction distinct meeting points are |A−B| and opposite are A+B when A,B are coprime integers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses k×L / relative speed for the k-th meeting and states the |A−B| / A+B meeting-point counts.

probes: How far does a train travel to pass a platform versus a standing person?
Given upstream and downstream speeds, how do you find boat and stream speeds?
When do two runners on a circular track meet for the k-th time?

hints.1: Ask what distance must be covered for the objects to clear each other.
hints.2: Trains: length (or sum of lengths) over relative speed; boats: with/against the current; circular: relative distance equals multiples of L.
hints.3: Platform pass uses L_train+L_platform; boats use u=(D+U)/2, v=(D−U)/2; k-th circular meeting when relative distance is k×L.

phases.goal: Choose the right averaging and shortcut methods instead of tempting but wrong shortcuts.

must_hit.point: For equal distances, harmonic-style average 2ab/(a+b) is correct; arithmetic mean of the two speeds is wrong because more time is spent at the slower speed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts 2ab/(a+b) with (a+b)/2 and explains the slower-speed time bias.

must_hit.point: For a shuttling fly or drone between closing objects, multiply continuous flight speed by total time to intercept instead of summing the infinite zig-zag series.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the Von Neumann fly / drone shortcut: distance = flyer speed × time until the hosts meet.

must_hit.point: On an up-escalator, walking faster makes you count more visible steps because you spend less time on it and the escalator contributes fewer steps.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains why the faster walker can report a larger step count on the same moving escalator.

probes: Why is the average of two speeds often wrong for a round trip?
Should you sum every leg of a shuttling fly, or is there a better approach?

hints.1: Think about what is held constant: distance, time, or continuous motion.
hints.2: Equal-distance journeys need harmonic averaging; infinite shuttles collapse to time × flyer speed.
hints.3: Use 2ab/(a+b) not (a+b)/2; for the fly, find collision time then multiply by fly speed.

phases.goal: Map disguised OA stories and classic puzzles back onto relative-speed and escalator models.

must_hit.point: OA wording with patrol robots, packets, or similar agents still maps to relative speed and joint distance covered between meetings.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Strips the story to closing/joint distance and relative speed, including reflection corridors when walls reverse direction.

must_hit.point: For a fly or drone shuttling until one vehicle catches another, total distance is flyer speed times the catch-up time from the head-start gap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Computes head-start gap, catch-up time at relative speed, then flyer_speed × that time.

must_hit.point: Escalator visible steps equal walker steps plus escalator steps during that time; equate two walkers' expressions for N to solve for the step-rate ratio.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sets N = steps_taken + escalator contribution and equates two rates to find N when the escalator is off.

probes: Two robots bounce between ends of a corridor—how do you find when they cross the second time?
A drone zig-zags between two trains until they meet—what distance does it fly?
How do you find how many escalator steps are visible when it is switched off?

hints.1: Ignore the story dressing and identify gap, relative speed, and what 'meeting' means.
hints.2: Corridor reflections often mean the n-th meeting corresponds to an odd multiple of corridor length in joint distance; shuttles use time × speed; escalators equate two expressions for N.
hints.3: Second corridor crossing uses joint distance 3D at relative speed; drone distance = drone speed × catch-up time; escalator N from equating the two walkers' N equations.

tradeoffs.topic: Arithmetic mean of speeds vs 2ab/(a+b) for equal distances
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Equal distances require average speed 2ab/(a+b). Averaging the speeds as (a+b)/2 overcounts the faster leg because more time is spent at the slower speed.

tradeoffs.topic: Summing infinite zig-zag legs vs flyer speed × intercept time
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Do not sum the infinite series of shuttle segments. Find the time until the hosts meet (or one catches the other), then multiply by the flyer's constant speed.

tradeoffs.topic: Faster vs slower walking on an up-escalator (steps counted)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Walking faster shortens time on the escalator, so the escalator contributes fewer steps and you must supply more—hence a faster walker can count more steps, not fewer.

gotchas.trap: Averaging equal-distance speeds as (40+60)/2 = 50 instead of using 2ab/(a+b).
gotchas.correction: Use average speed = 2ab/(a+b); more time is spent at the slower speed, so the true average is pulled toward it.

gotchas.trap: Summing an infinite geometric series of drone or fly zig-zags between closing trains.
gotchas.correction: Compute total time until intercept from the head-start gap and relative speed, then multiply by the flyer’s constant speed.

gotchas.trap: Assuming walking faster on an up-escalator means you count fewer steps.
gotchas.correction: Faster walking means less time on the escalator, so it lifts you fewer steps and you count more of your own steps.

gotchas.trap: Treating average speed as the mean of segment speeds when distances (or times) are unequal without computing total distance over total time.
gotchas.correction: Always use total distance / total time; only the equal-distance two-speed case collapses neatly to 2ab/(a+b).
